A grown fae in a scarlet petal-silk tunic hauls on both oars while a dormouse braces in the bow with the mooring line in his paws; a beetle rides the thwart between them, going along with it.
A grown fae in leaf-cloth kneels to steer with a reed paddle, a hedgehog wedged against her knee bailing with half a nutshell, and a wren perched on her shoulder calling the line ahead.
A grown fae in moss-velvet leans far out over the water to hold a turn, one hand on the rail, while a frog sits square in the stern as ballast and a field mouse hangs onto the mast behind her.
A grown fae with cropped violet hair poles hard off the streambed, a vole hauling the sheet in front of her and a newt draped along the gunwale steering with his tail in the water.
A grown fae in gold-shot leaf-cloth stands at the oars mid-stroke, spray coming over her; a dormouse in an acorn-cap helmet crouches at her feet gripping the thwart with both paws.
A grown fae in plum petal-silk shares her hull with two field mice, one rowing opposite her and one sitting in the bow eating a berry and contributing nothing.
A grown fae in woven-grass jerkin laughs as she rows, a bullfrog at her stern with his throat pouch full and a damselfly riding the bow like a figurehead.
A grown fae in cream petal-silk trims her sail one-handed while a red squirrel holds his tail up as a spare sail behind her and a snail makes slow progress along the gunwale.
A grown fae in indigo leaf-cloth throws her weight against the tiller, a hedgehog and a wren crammed in the bow with her, both leaning the same way.
A grown fae in flame-orange petal-silk shouts back at the fleet over her shoulder; a mole in dark velvet rows steadily beside her with no idea what she is shouting about.
A grown fae in sage leaf-cloth takes the long clean line, a toad sitting immovable amidships and a cricket fiddling from the stern where he was told not to sit.
A grown fae in cherry petal-silk hangs off her mast one-handed to clear a snagged line while a frog below holds the boat steady against the reeds with both webbed hands.
A grown fae in white petal-silk with luna-moth wings folded back rows a full boat-length clear, a dormouse asleep in the bow and a beetle keeping watch for her.
A grown fae in copper leaf-cloth tries to pry a crayfish off her own rudder while a water shrew swims alongside offering advice she cannot use.
A grown fae in teal leaf-cloth is thrown backwards as a diving beetle surfaces under the bow, her wings flaring to catch herself, a vole in the stern pointing and delighted.
A grown fae in pearl petal-silk kneels low to trim the hull flat, a harvest mouse coiled around the mast beside her with his tail wrapped twice for grip.
A grown fae in russet leaf-cloth reaches out to catch a wood frog mid-leap between her boat and the next, a dormouse behind her covering his eyes.
A grown fae in saffron petal-silk rows with real effort while a water rat at her stern steers with one paw and the calm of a professional.
A grown fae in olive leaf-cloth ships her oars to coast, a duckling paddling furiously alongside to keep up and a wagtail running the bank calling the race.
A grown fae in rose-petal cape tips half out of her hull holding on by one hand, a hedgehog braced against the far rail as a counterweight.
A grown fae in marigold petal-silk stands on her thwart with both arms flung wide, a frog and a mouse on either side of her holding the boat level.
A grown fae in deep-blue petal-silk crosses her arms at the very bow while a dormouse does all the hauling behind her and a robin keeps station overhead.
A grown fae in amber leaf-cloth bails fast with a thimble, water coming in faster, a shrew rowing beside her and a kingfisher on the mast declining to help.
A grown fae in silver-grey petal-silk steers with a twig tiller, a rabbit filling most of the boat behind her with his ears flat in the wind.
A grown fae in bronze leaf-cloth and a stag beetle share one oar each, pulling in perfect time, a newt riding between them as ballast.

A wiry amber-skinned fae with coiled red hair and beetle-iridescent wings in a tunic of overlapping poppy petals who cheats by cutting the rowanberry turn and grins; a silver-braided elder in plum moss-velvet who never hurries and arrives first; and a bright scatter of fae in marigold, cream and berry-red behind, wings catching spray — one snail keeping steady pace along the bank and pulling ahead.

A broad cheerful dark-skinned fae with moth-soft wings and grass-cord sash who rows sitting backwards shouting encouragement to rivals; a pale terrified young one in woven grass clutching her acorn-cup cap with both hands; and behind them a loose field of fae in scarlet, plum and copper leaf-cloth, sleeves pushed back, bare feet braced wide.

Two tall sisters with long black hair and butterfly-patterned wings in matching moss-velvet who bicker the entire length of the course without pausing to steer; a calm brown-skinned elder in bark-fibre who has plainly already won; and a field of young fae in kilted-up petal-silk, every colour, strung out behind like scattered petals.

A very small pale fae in an acorn-cup cap and a single folded-leaf tunic, plainly horrified to be racing at all, gripping her twig mast with both arms; a heavyset copper-skinned one with silver braids and beetle wings in bark-fibre rowing a hull twice her size; and behind them a dozen fae in plum, cream and ivy-green, all barefoot.

A freckled golden fae with cropped white hair and birch-seed translucent wings in a rose-petal cloak who steers using only a trailing bare foot; a long-limbed dark fae in woven grass poling hard from the stern with a peeled twig; and a loose mixed field in scarlet and marigold petal-silk, the oldest silver-haired and fastest of them all.

A lean russet-haired fae with dragonfly-clear wings in a scarlet petal-silk tunic who stands straight upright at the bow throughout; a round-faced young one in green leaf-cloth with moth-dusted wings who has stowed a small newt under the thwart as ballast and refuses to explain; and a field of fae in cream, copper and plum strung out cheerfully behind.

A heavyset laughing fae with dark cropped hair and iridescent beetle wings in a broad-shouldered bark-fibre tunic who rows the wrong direction on one side; a solemn silver-haired elder in plum petal-silk who corrects nobody and wins; and a bright varied scatter of fae in moss-green, scarlet and marigold, wings of every kind, ages from very young to oldest.

A deep-brown-skinned fae with long loose hair and moth-soft dusted wings in woven grass kilted at the knee who never blinks and never loses; a pale young one in a cloak of linked violet petals who is clearly racing her hull for the first time and finding it thrilling; and a field behind them in berry-red, plum and cream, all barefoot.

A pair of small cousins with matching copper braids and patterned butterfly wings sharing one leaf-cloth hull, arguing with great passion about who is steering; a calm tall fae with cool brown skin and birch-seed wings in bark-fibre who ignores them and glides through; and a scatter of fae in ivy, scarlet and marigold behind, the oldest grinning widest.

A reckless amber-haired fae with clear dragonfly wings in a marigold petal-silk tunic who stands on the rim of the hull for speed and tips dangerously left; a serene dark-skinned elder in moss-velvet with silver-shot locs who has seen this before and sails through the gap; and behind them a varied field in plum, cream and copper, wings bright with spray.

A tiny pale fae with a white braid wound twice around and moth-soft wings in a woven-grass tunic three sizes large, sleeves rolled to the elbow, bailing with an acorn cap she also wears as a hat; a broad golden-skinned fae in scarlet leaf-cloth who cheats at the twig-arch gate and blows a kiss back; and a loose field in plum and marigold behind.

A long-limbed cool-toned fae with straight black hair and iridescent wings in bark-fibre, one bare foot on the rudder twig, reading the current with her eyes closed; a freckled young one in a rose-petal cloak who is racing a hull far too large and absolutely delighted about it; and a field of fae in cream, berry-red and moss-green scattered behind.

A stout copper-skinned fae with cropped silver hair and dusted moth wings in a cloak of overlapping seed-cases who never hurries and is somehow always first through the rowanberry turn; a young dark fae in grass-plaited green standing up to pole and wobbling magnificently; and behind them a bright mixed field in scarlet, plum and marigold, wings of four kinds, all bare feet.

A willowy pale fae with long auburn hair and birch-seed wings in a plum petal-silk tunic who sails standing and absolutely silent, face unreadable; two small dark-haired fae in matching leaf-cloth who bicker without ceasing and steer by accident; and a field of fae in copper, cream and ivy-green strung out behind, the silver-haired elder at the back overtaking everyone quietly.

A broad-shouldered warm-toned fae with close-cropped hair and beetle-iridescent wings in a grass-sash tunic who rows with great force in entirely the wrong direction before correcting; a slender white-haired elder in deep plum moss-velvet with dragonfly-clear wings who arrives first regardless; and behind them a loose cheerful field in scarlet, berry-red and marigold, every hull tipping, every wing catching spray.

A freckled fae with short russet hair and patterned butterfly wings in a single ivy-leaf tunic who cheats at the twig-arch gate, grins, and immediately does it again; a grave tall fae with cool dark skin and birch-seed wings in woven grass who sails without speaking; and a varied field in plum, cream and copper behind, young to silver-haired, all kilted up.

A warm brown-skinned fae with heavy coiled hair and moth-soft wings in a bark-fibre tunic, utterly terrified, eyes wide, holding the twig mast with both hands and both knees; a cheerful silver-haired elder in marigold petal-silk who shouts encouragement across the water to everyone including rivals; and behind them a field in scarlet, plum and moss-green, wings of every pattern, all barefoot.

A golden-skinned fae with loose white hair and beetle-iridescent wings in overlapping rose-petal layers, up to the knee in her own flooded hull and still the one to beat; a thin dark fae in woven grass with birch-seed wings who steers by leaning alone and has never needed more; and a bright scatter behind in cream, copper and berry-red, oldest racer leading the pack.

A small pale fae with silver braids and clear dragonfly wings in a scarlet tunic of one wide poppy petal, sleeves pushed well back, who cheats by blowing rivals off course with a fan of birch bark, then fans them back and winks; a serene dark-skinned fae in moss-velvet who pays no attention and wins; and a loose field in marigold, plum and green behind.

Two amber-skinned brothers with long braided hair and iridescent wings in bark-fibre tunics who race together and argue every stroke; a calm pale elder with cropped silver hair and moth-soft wings in woven grass who glides between them saying nothing; and behind, a field of fae in berry-red, cream and plum, some very young and barely steering, one snail at the bank overtaking all.

A reckless young fae with dark curling hair and butterfly-patterned wings in a grass-sash tunic who stands on the bow with arms out and tips sharply right mid-course; a warm-toned elder with long silver hair and dragonfly-clear wings in deep plum bark-fibre who has watched this for decades and arrives first; and a loose field in scarlet, marigold and ivy, all in fae-craft cloth.

A heavyset cool-skinned fae with a wide braid and moth-dusted wings in a leaf-cloth tunic kilted at the hip who rows a hull far too large with enormous enjoyment; a willowy copper-haired fae in petal-silk standing and poling with a peeled twig as though it is obvious; and behind them a varied scatter in plum, cream and marigold, the youngest barely visible over the rim.

A pale fae with a long white plait and birch-seed wings in a moss-velvet tunic, plainly the calmest fae on the water, who never hurries and keeps winning to everyone's frustration; a laughing dark-skinned young one in a scarlet petal-silk cloak who tries to cut the rowanberry turn and misjudges it delightfully; and a field behind in copper, berry-red and cream, all covered, all barefoot.

A stout warm brown fae with short curling hair and iridescent beetle wings in woven grass and a grass-cord belt who steers with a bare foot on the twig rudder and both hands free to wave at the crowd; a solemn young pale fae in bark-fibre with clear wings who rows in total silence; and a bright field in plum, marigold and ivy behind them.

A lean dark-skinned fae with close-cropped hair and dragonfly-clear wings in overlapping seed-case armour, reckless, hull tipping at every gate; a broad silver-haired elder in cream petal-silk with moth-soft wings who cheats so gracefully no one minds; and behind them a scatter of fae in scarlet, berry-red and plum, ages ranging from a tiny one in an acorn-cup cap to a weathered elder.

A small freckled fae with bright auburn hair and butterfly-patterned wings in a rose-petal cloak, clearly terrified, who is racing a hull twice her length with visible determination; a tall grave copper-skinned fae in bark-fibre with birch-seed wings who says nothing and steers everything correctly; and a field of fae in moss-green, marigold and cream strung out behind, the silver-haired ones fastest.

A broad golden fae with heavy silver-shot braids and iridescent wings in deep plum moss-velvet who rows sitting backwards and gives advice to every fae she passes; a slight pale young one in woven grass with moth-soft wings who has lashed a dandelion seed to the bow as a spare sail and is very pleased with this; and a varied field in scarlet, cream and copper behind.

A wiry dark fae with long loose hair and clear dragonfly wings in a marigold petal-silk tunic who stands the entire race and tilts the hull with each shift of weight; a calm warm-toned elder in bark-fibre with silver hair wound up and beetle-iridescent wings who arrives first without appearing to move quickly; and behind them a loose bright field in plum, berry-red and ivy, all bare feet.

A pale round-faced young fae in a cloak of overlapping violet petals and moth-soft wings, clearly bewildered by the current; a lean dark-skinned silver-haired fae in scarlet petal-silk with birch-seed wings who steers by leaning and has never once touched a paddle; and a cheerful varied field behind in cream, copper and marigold, the smallest fae at the back towing a walnut-shell tender holding one sleepy frog.

A cool-skinned fae with cropped dark hair and patterned butterfly wings in woven grass, sleeves pushed to the shoulder, who cheats at the twig arch by ducking under it backwards and laughing; a serene broad elder with long silver hair and moth-dusted wings in plum bark-fibre who needs no such tricks; and behind them a scatter in scarlet, berry-red and marigold, young to ancient, every wing a different kind.

A wiry amber-skinned fae with short copper braids and dragonfly-clear wings in a saffron petal-silk tunic, racing standing on the stern and howling; a long-limbed silver-haired one in bark-fibre who never raises her voice and keeps winning; a terrified tiny one in woven grass gripping her twig mast with both fists; and behind them fae in plum, berry-red and cream — a snail keeping perfect pace along the bank and beating half of them.

Two bickering cousins with wild black curls and matching moss-velvet, beetle-iridescent wings cracking with argument the whole length of the course; a calm bronze-skinned fae in overlapping rose-petal cloak who steers with one bare foot and says nothing; and a field of fae in kilted leaf-cloth, sleeves pushed back, spread bright as scattered petals across the water.

A heavyset elder fae with silver braids and moth-dusted wings in deep plum bark-fibre, rowing a hull far too large, absolutely delighted; a freckled pale one in an acorn-cup cap and woven-grass sash who cheats charmingly and grins; and the rest bright in marigold, jade and berry behind — a dandelion seed snagged to the elder's stern working perfectly as a spare sail.

A tall dark-skinned fae with long locked hair and birch-seed translucent wings in scarlet petal-silk, sailing perfectly upright and silent; a very small warm-brown one in a single-leaf tunic, plainly terrified, bailing with an acorn cap; and behind them a cheerful scatter of fae in cream, copper and soft gold, wings catching spray, bare feet braced on thwarts.

A lean pale fae with cropped white hair and butterfly-patterned wings in a grass-cord-belted leaf tunic, poling from the stern with one long reed; a round-faced young one in moss-velvet whose hull tilts so far the water comes in; and a field of varied fae, warm-skinned to cool, old to young, in petal-silk of every committed colour strung out behind.

A broad cheerful fae with auburn waves and moth-soft wings in green leaf-cloth, rowing backwards and offering loud advice to everyone; a grave olive-skinned one with a heavy plait and clear dragonfly wings in plum petal-silk who accepts no advice; and a loose field in woven grass, bark-fibre and berry-red silk — a beetle riding unmoved under one thwart through the whole chaos.

A golden-skinned fae with cropped red hair and iridescent beetle wings, kilted-up petal-silk and knees soaked, still racing with her hull half full; a silvery elder in bark-fibre and birch-seed wings who never hurries and keeps arriving first; and behind them a bright scatter of young fae in rose, jade and saffron, faces vivid, bare feet gripping wet thwarts hard.

A very small fae with long copper hair and translucent wings in a woven-grass tunic, racing a hull three times her size with furious dignity; a tall cool-skinned one in a cloak of overlapping violet petals who cheats beautifully and waves as he passes; and the rest of the field in leaf-cloth and petal-silk, plum and cream and marigold, wings all catching spray.

A dark-haired warm-brown fae in saffron petal-silk with dragonfly-clear wings who sails standing and silent; a pair of small pale-skinned fae in matching woven grass who share one paddle and bicker in fierce whispers; and behind them a wide bright field from the very young to the silver-haired — a walnut-shell tender towed on a grass line carrying a mouse as ballast.

A broad silver-haired fae with deep brown skin and moth-dusted wings in deep green moss-velvet, clearly cheating and clearly winning; a terrified freckled young one in an acorn-cup cap, both hands on the mast, eyes closed; and a long field of fae behind in bark-fibre and petal-silk, every colour from cream to scarlet, wings raised bright against the spray.

A wiry pale fae with long white braids and butterfly-patterned wings in a bark-fibre tunic belted with plaited grass, poling with one foot on the hull's edge; a warm-gold-skinned young one in rose petal-silk who has plainly never raced before and is thrilled; and a varied field in kilted leaf-cloth and woven grass behind, faces bright, bare feet braced wide.

A lean dark-skinned fae with short black hair and dragonfly-clear wings in berry-red petal-silk, steering with one bare foot on the rudder bar and grinning; a heavyset elder in overlapping oak-leaf cloak with silver wings who rows vast slow powerful strokes; and a field of bright fae in jade, marigold and cream behind — a boot-shaped seed-pod bailed out mid-race with a broken acorn cap.

Two tall sisters with long amber hair and matched birch-seed wings in contrasting petal-silk, bickering at full voice the whole length of the course; a small cool-skinned elder in plum moss-velvet who says nothing and keeps winning; and behind them a scatter of fae in woven grass and bark-fibre, from the very tiny to the broad-shouldered, wings all different.

A round-faced warm-brown young fae in a single broad-petal cloak who steers by leaning and has no other plan; a lean copper-haired one in scarlet leaf-cloth with moth-soft wings who sails standing, arms out for balance; and behind them a long bright field of fae in plum, cream and saffron — a snail on the bank overtaking four of them by the far bend.

A heavyset pale fae with silver-streaked black hair and iridescent wings in deep jade petal-silk, rowing a hull twice his size with cheerful imprecision; a slight golden-skinned one in woven grass, perfectly calm, never raising her paddle, always ahead; and the field behind in leaf-cloth and bark-fibre in every saturated colour, sleeves pushed back, spray bright on their faces.

A freckled red-haired fae in a tunic cut from one folded ivy leaf, birch-seed wings, cheating so openly it becomes charming; a tall brown-skinned grave one in plum petal-silk with dragonfly wings who sails straight and silent and ignores the cheating; and a varied young field in woven grass and moss-velvet, cream to copper, old enough to know better and young enough not to care.

A tiny cool-skinned fae with long white hair and butterfly wings in a woven-grass tunic, plainly terrified, steering by accident; a broad warm-brown elder in bark-fibre and moth-dusted wings who rows backwards and shouts encouragement at the terrified one; and behind them a bright chaos of fae in rose, jade and marigold — a dandelion seed tied to the tiny one's mast pulling her slowly forward.

A long-limbed amber-skinned fae with cropped hair and dragonfly-clear wings in saffron petal-silk who poles standing at the hull's stern, leaning far out; a small pale one in a cloak of linked violet petals who is clearly bailing and clearly losing; and a field of fae behind in leaf-cloth and bark-fibre, silver-haired to very young, every wing kind catching the spray.

A grave dark-eyed fae with long black hair and beetle-iridescent wings in plum moss-velvet who sails standing and has not smiled once; a cheerful broad one with red braids and moth-soft wings in green leaf-cloth who is losing magnificently and enjoying it; and behind them a scatter from cream to berry-red, fae of every build and age, kilted and barefoot, wings up.

A slight warm-brown fae with silver braids and birch-seed wings in a bark-fibre tunic, calm and precise, arriving first by doing least; a very young pale one in saffron petal-silk who stands up in excitement and immediately tips in; and a bright field in woven grass and rose petal-silk behind, the far ones small but vivid — a newt riding one hull's prow, steady and self-important.

Two bickering pale fae with different-length auburn hair and contrasting moth-soft wings in matching woven-grass tunics, paddling in furiously wrong directions; a lean dark-skinned elder in a cloak of overlapping birch-bark pieces with dragonfly wings, amused, still winning; and a long varied field in berry-red, jade and cream behind, sleeves pushed back, bare feet gripping every thwart.

A broad golden-skinned fae with long loose black hair and butterfly-patterned wings in scarlet petal-silk, cheating lavishly, waving at the crowd as she passes; a wiry pale one in a woven-grass sash and bark-fibre tunic who sails standing without speaking; and a field of fae in plum, marigold and soft gold, old to young, every wing variety, all kilted and barefoot.

A small cool-skinned fae with cropped silver hair and translucent wings in jade petal-silk, racing a hull far too large, managing by sheer stubbornness; a tall warm-brown one with long braids and moth-dusted wings in deep rose bark-fibre who steers with one foot and reads the water; and the field behind in cream, plum and copper — a dragonfly pacing the leader the whole way.

A heavyset elder fae with amber skin and short copper hair, iridescent wings, in an oak-leaf cloak belted with grass cord, rowing with enormous calm authority; a tiny freckled one in woven grass and acorn-cup cap who has entered a hull plainly designed for someone else; and a bright scattered field of fae in petal-silk behind, scarlet to cream, very young to very old.

A lean dark-skinned fae with long locked hair and dragonfly-clear wings in berry-red leaf-cloth, poling from the hull's stern with her eyes on the far twig-arch; a pale round-faced young one in moss-velvet whose hull tilts left and stays there; and behind them a vivid field in jade, saffron and plum, fae of every build, wings all different, spray on every face.

A wiry warm-brown fae with short white hair and moth-soft wings in a cloak of overlapping rose petals, cheating with such grace that three boats simply let her past; a grave long-limbed pale one in plum petal-silk and birch-seed wings who rows in measured silence; and the rest a bright diverse scatter in woven grass and bark-fibre, old to very young, sleeves pushed back.

A freckled pale fae with copper braids and butterfly-patterned wings in saffron petal-silk, up to her knees in a flooding hull and still racing; a calm broad dark-skinned one in green moss-velvet and dragonfly-clear wings who has never hurried once in her life and keeps winning; and a long field in berry-red, cream and marigold behind — one hull towing a walnut shell with a fieldmouse inside.

Two small pale cousins with mismatched dark and fair hair sharing one paddle, both in woven grass, bickering in fierce undertones the whole course; a tall amber-skinned elder with silver braids and iridescent wings in deep plum bark-fibre who sails straight past them both without looking; and a vivid field in rose, jade and copper behind, young fae to very old, all bare feet.

A bold dark-skinned fae with cropped red hair and dragonfly wings in a scarlet single-petal cloak, rowing standing and shouting; a terrified small pale one in woven grass gripping both sides of a hull too wide to grip; and behind them a field in bark-fibre, petal-silk and leaf-cloth from cream to deep plum — a snail ahead of five of them before the first twig-arch.

A long-limbed cool-skinned fae with silver-streaked black hair and birch-seed wings in deep jade petal-silk, sailing with her eyes shut and her face turned up; a broad warm-gold elder in moss-velvet and moth-dusted wings rowing powerfully backwards; a tiny young one in saffron woven-grass barely visible over her hull's edge; and a bright chaotic field in plum, scarlet and cream, wings up, bare feet braced.

A stocky amber-skinned fae with copper braids and beetle-iridescent wings in moss-velvet, rowing furiously with eyes shut; a willowy one in plum petal-silk with birch-seed wings who steers barefoot and arrives first without seeming to hurry; and behind them a bright scatter of fae in marigold, cream and berry-red leaf-cloth — one trailing a dandelion seed as a spare sail.

A silver-haired fae in bark-fibre with moth-dusted wings who cheats charmingly at every twig-arch gate and grins wide; a very small dark-eyed one in woven grass, plainly terrified, gripping her mast with both fists; and a loose field of fae from young to ancient, wings flashing dragonfly-clear and butterfly-patterned across the spray.

Two tall sisters with long red hair and matching scarlet petal-silk who bicker the whole course, paddles clashing; a calm broad fae in green leaf-cloth with iridescent wings who never speaks and keeps winning; and a field of smaller fae in plum, gold and white behind, a snail keeping perfect pace along the bank unnoticed.

A lean dark-skinned fae with cropped white hair and birch-seed wings, sleeves shoved back, bailing with an acorn cap while still in the lead; a heavyset elder with silver braids and moth-soft wings rowing a hull far too vast for him; and a cheerful crowd in bark-fibre and woven grass spread wide behind.

A freckled pale fae in a cloak of overlapping violet petals who cheats by leaning on a reed at the turn and laughs; a grave long-limbed one in plum bark-fibre with dragonfly-clear wings who sails standing and silent; and the rest a bright tangle in cream, moss-green and marigold, wings every kind.

A tiny golden fae in an acorn-cup cap and woven grass who is racing a hull twice her size by sheer indignant will; a cool brown-skinned one in birch-bark fibre with clear wings who steers with one bare foot and watches everything; and a field in leaf-cloth of jade, scarlet and amber streaming behind, varied and loud.

A broad cheerful fae with rust-coloured curls and moth-dusted wings in moss-velvet who shouts encouragement at every rival including the frog watching from a lily pad; a slender young one in rose petal-silk, white-haired, clearly terrified, eyes enormous; and a scatter of elder fae in bark-fibre and woven grass, silver-braided, competitive and absolutely silent.

A dark-eyed fae with long black hair and butterfly-patterned wings in woven grass who steers barefoot and hums; a reckless copper-skinned one in marigold leaf-cloth with iridescent wings who takes every gate too fast and tips; and behind them a field of fae from very young to silver-haired, a walnut hull trailing a mouse on a grass cord used as ballast.

A calm elder fae with white braids and birch-seed wings in bark-fibre who has plainly won this before and shows it in every unhurried stroke; a small panicked one in acorn-green petal-silk with clear wings clutching a twig mast; and the rest a riot of cream, cobalt and berry, wings loud in the spray.

A willowy bronze-skinned fae in a tunic cut from one broad sycamore leaf with moth-soft wings, poling from the stern and singing; a compact freckled one in scarlet petal-silk with beetle wings who cheats cheerfully at the rowanberry turn; and behind, a varied scatter in plum, bark-gold and jade, the youngest fae still tying a grass cord at the waist while racing.

A heavyset warm-skinned fae with close-cropped black hair and iridescent wings in deep moss-velvet rowing sitting backwards and narrating everything loudly; a grave slender one in white petal-silk with birch-seed wings who neither speaks nor loses; and a field of bright fae behind in every wing-kind from dusted moth to clear dragonfly, a beetle stowed visibly under one thwart.

A pair of small cousins with tawny skin and matching woven-grass tunics sharing a single paddle and arguing over every stroke; a tall silver-haired fae in bark-fibre with clear wings who watches them with amusement and still wins; and a loose crowd in scarlet, plum and cream behind, bare feet braced, sleeves pushed high.

A reckless amber fae with short copper hair and butterfly wings in marigold leaf-cloth who has lost her paddle and is using a broad leaf; a calm dark-skinned elder in plum moss-velvet with moth-dusted wings who rows one stroke and glides three; and the rest a brilliant field in bark-fibre, petal-silk and woven grass, varied in every colour.

A very young fae with a tumble of white curls and pale freckled skin in rose petal-silk with oversized birch-seed wings going the wrong way entirely, joyful about it; a brown-skinned composed one in green leaf-cloth with clear wings who corrects course for nobody; and behind a field of older fae in gold, berry and shadow-plum, silver-haired and swift.

A lean warm-brown fae with a long dark plait and dragonfly-clear wings in scarlet bark-fibre who cheats by drafting the leader's wake and winks; a broad elder fae with silver curls and iridescent wings in deep moss-velvet who rows in absolute silence and absolute fury; and a field of bright young fae behind in petal-silk of cream, jade and fire.
